question_text: A 58-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his family because of severe upper back pain, which he describes as ripping. His temperature is 36.5°C (97.7°F), the heart rate is 110/min and the blood pressure is 182/81 mm Hg in the right arm and 155/71 mm Hg in the left arm. CT scan of the chest shows an intimal flap limited to the descending aorta. Intravenous opioid analgesia is started. Which of the following is the best next step in the management of this patient condition?

                    ### Question
                    A 58-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his family because of severe upper back pain, which he describes as ripping. He denies the use of nicotine, alcohol or illicit drugs. Which of the following is the best next step in the management of this patient condition?

Immediate management focuses on blood pressure control to prevent complications such as rupture or organ ischemia. Intravenous esmolol is preferred in this acute setting due to its rapid onset and ability to effectively lower both heart rate and blood pressure. Other options, such as oral metoprolol or sublingual nitroglycerin, are less suitable for immediate management of aortic dissection. The evidence paths regarding hypertension and its relationship to aortic dissection support the need for urgent blood pressure management. Therefore, intravenous esmolol is the best next step in this patient's management.
